{{Short description|Concept in game theory involving long-term strategic planning}}
In [[game theory]], '''farsightness''' refers to players’ ability to consider the long-term consequences of their strategies, beyond immediate payoffs, often formalized as '''farsighted stability''' where players anticipate future moves and stable outcomes.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Chwe |first=Michael Suk-Young |year=1994 |title=Farsighted Coalitional Stability |journal=Journal of Economic Theory |volume=63 |issue=2 |pages=299–325 |doi=10.1006/jeth.1994.1044}}</ref> 

In static games, players optimize payoffs based on current information, as in the [[Nash equilibrium]],<ref>{{Cite book |last=Fudenberg |first=Drew |last2=Tirole |first2=Jean |title=Game Theory |publisher=MIT Press |year=1991 |isbn=978-0-262-06141-4 |pages=18-20}}</ref> but farsightedness involves anticipating [[Dynamic game|dynamic]] or [[Repeated game|repeated]] interactions, such as in coalition games like [[hedonic games]] where preferences shape long-term alliances.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last=Bogomolnaia |first=Anna |last2=Jackson |first2=Matthew O. |title=The Stability of Hedonic Coalition Structures |journal=Games and Economic Behavior |volume=38 |issue=2 |year=2002 |pages=201–230 |doi=10.1006/game.2001.0877}}</ref> For example, in a repeated [[Prisoner's Dilemma]], a farsighted player might cooperate to encourage future cooperation, unlike the one-shot case where defection prevails.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Maynard Smith |first=John |title=Evolution and the Theory of Games |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=1982 |isbn=978-0-521-28884-2 |page=56}}</ref> Similarly, a player might refuse a small immediate payoff to build a more valuable alliance later.<ref name=":0" />

Farsightedness assumes significant foresight and computational ability, which may be unrealistic in complex scenarios. In evolutionary settings, myopic strategies might dominate if immediate survival outweighs long-term planning.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Maynard Smith |first=John |title=Evolution and the Theory of Games |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=1982 |isbn=978-0-521-28884-2 |page=34}}</ref> 

== Applications ==
In [[evolutionary game theory]], farsightedness contrasts with myopic adaptation, where strategies adjust based on immediate fitness.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Maynard Smith |first=John |title=Evolution and the Theory of Games |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=1982 |isbn=978-0-521-28884-2 |pages=20-23}}</ref> A farsighted strategy might aim for an [[evolutionarily stable strategy]] (ESS) that withstands long-term mutant challenges. In coalition settings, farsighted players assess how current choices affect future stability, rejecting short-term gains for long-term benefits, as seen in hedonic games.<ref name=":1" /> Farsighted stability captures this by modeling chains of responses predicting stable configurations.<ref name=":0" />
